choices.text: Yes: if it is a metal, a magnet will pull it
No: a magnet only pulls iron and a few metals, and ignores most other metals
Yes: a magnet pulls every object, metal or not

questions.explanation: The trap is: A magnet attracts every kind of metal. Scene s4 shows why this is wrong: Magnets ignore most things: they only pull iron and a few metals.
questions.misconception: A magnet attracts every kind of metal.
questions.prompt: A pupil says a magnet will attract any metal object. What is wrong with this idea?

choices.text: A push, because the box moves across the table
A pull, because the box is brought closer to the child
Friction, because the box is sliding

questions.explanation: Scene s1: a pull brings something closer, while a push moves it away - the box is dragged towards the child, so it is a pull.
questions.prompt: A child drags a box towards herself across the floor. Which force is she using?

questions.answer: Friction is the rubbing force between the block and the rough surface; it pushes back against the slide and slows the block down.
questions.explanation: Scene s2: the rough surface rubs against the sliding block - that rubbing force is friction, and it acts against the movement, slowing the block.
questions.prompt: A block slides down a rough slope and slows down. Name the force that slows it and explain how it works.

questions.answer: They attract: the magnets pull together and snap onto each other.
questions.explanation: Scene s3: opposite poles attract - when S faces N the magnets pull each other and snap together with a click.
questions.prompt: The south pole of one magnet is brought near the north pole of another magnet. What happens, and why?

choices.text: They push each other apart and repel
Nothing: magnets only work when they are touching

questions.explanation: Scene s4: turn the magnet around so N faces N - like poles repel, and the magnets push each other apart.
questions.prompt: Two magnets are brought together with their north poles facing each other. What happens?
